passage: I'm Tanvir. Whenever my little brother reached for my model cars, Mummy said, "Share, he is younger." Every single time. I went quiet, my anger a hard little ball. When Damini Masi visited, she noticed my scowl. "Fair is not always the same as equal," she said. I told her the plain cars were fine to share but the painted ones were mine. She said I should tell Mummy exactly that. So I did: "These three I can share. These I can't." Mummy paused. "That's reasonable," she said. I still get annoyed sometimes, but now I say it out loud instead of going silent. 🙂

qa.q: What did Mummy say whenever Tanvir's brother reached for the cars?
What was Tanvir feeling when going quiet each time the order to share came?
qa.a: Tanvir felt the rule was unfair and kept the anger inside like a hard little ball.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do to make the sharing fairer?
qa.a: Tanvir told Mummy exactly which cars could be shared and which were not, and she agreed it was reasonable.

qa.q: How might Mummy have seen Tanvir's silence before the explanation?
qa.a: She may have thought Tanvir was fine with sharing, since Tanvir said nothing; the explanation helped her see what was fair.

grounding: A child resents being told to share because a brother is younger, then explains which items can be lent.

passage:
I'm Vaibhav, and last year I was tired of hearing one sentence. Whenever my little brother Rinku grabbed my cricket bat or my comic books, my mother Devika said, "Share. He's younger."
It felt so unfair. I started keeping quiet and angry, and slammed my cupboard door.
One evening I finally said it. "Ma, I don't mind sharing some things. But not my bat, it cracks if he hits stones with it. And not my comics, he tears the pages. He can have my old football and my puzzle."
Ma looked at me for a long time. "That's fair. I should have asked what you think."
The cupboard door has been much quieter since.

qa.q: What did Ma usually say when Rinku grabbed Vaibhav's things?
How did Vaibhav feel about always having to share?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt it was unfair and grew quietly angry, slamming the cupboard door.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped?
qa.a: Vaibhav explained calmly which things were not okay to lend and which things Rinku could have, and asked to be treated fairly.

qa.q: How might Devika see things after Vaibhav spoke up?
qa.a: Devika saw it was fair and realised she should have asked first.

grounding: A child told to share because the brother is younger feels it is unfair, then explains to the mother what is not okay to lend and what can be shared.

passage:
Note from Vandana Masi, who looks after the boys after school.
Mohit (11) has been sulking for weeks. His younger brother Chintu keeps taking his colour pencils, and every time Mohit complains, his parents say, "He's little, let him have them."
Today Mohit refused to eat his snack and sat at the window, arms folded.
I asked what was wrong. He said, "Nobody listens to me. It's always Chintu."
I suggested he tell his parents what was okay to share and what wasn't. He wrote a list: "Okay: old crayons, board games. Not okay: new pencils." That evening he showed it to his parents. They listened and agreed.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling at the window with his arms folded?
qa.a: He felt resentful and unheard, believing it was always about Chintu.

qa.q: What helped Mohit instead of sulking?
qa.a: Vandana Masi suggested a list of what was okay to share, and Mohit showed it to his parents, who listened and agreed.

qa.q: How might Mohit's parents see the list?
qa.a: They seem to see it as a fair request, since they listened and agreed.

grounding: A boy resents being told to share because his brother is younger; a caregiver helps him explain what is okay to lend, and his parents agree.
